metadata.title: YWC GBV Indicator Evidence Base
metadata.source: Open North Synthesis (Sept 2025) + Boreal Logic v2 Expansion (Jan 2026)
metadata.prepared_for: Delphi Validation Study (Track A + Track B)

CC01.name: Housing market pressure index
CC01.definition: Impact of market trends (AirBnB, mining camps, speculation) on rental availability
CC01.definition_plain: How much pressure is there on the housing market from things like AirBnB and mining?
CC01.domain_question: Can survivors access emergency and transitional housing?
CC01.evidence_summary: Market forces (AirBnB, mining camps, speculation) affect housing availability for survivors.
risk_factors: Inflated housing costs due to resource development (Flynn, 2023)
Inflated housing due to gentrification, short-term rentals (Mantler, 2024)
CC01.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - composite from multiple sources.

CC02.name: RRN-specific cost burdens
CC02.definition: Additional costs faced by survivors in RRN contexts
CC02.definition_plain: How much extra does it cost survivors to live in a rural, remote or northern area (e.g., fuel, animal care, travel)?
CC02.tier_rationale: PATHWAY-CRITICAL: Extreme RRN costs can make leaving economically impossible
CC02.domain_question: Can survivors access money and resources to leave?
CC02.evidence_summary: Higher costs of living in RRN contexts increase financial barriers to leaving abuse.
risk_factors: Financial burdens unique to RRN communities (transportation, fuel, animal care) (Giesbrecht, 2022; Wuerch, 2021)
protective_factors: Financial support that accounts for RRN cost burdens
CC02.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - derived estimate from cost-of-living data.

CC03.name: Childcare availability and accessibility
CC03.definition: Access to licensed childcare as economic independence enabler
CC03.definition_plain: How available is childcare for parents trying to become independent?
CC03.tier_rationale: PATHWAY-CRITICAL: No childcare = cannot work = cannot sustain independence
CC03.domain_question: Can survivors access money and resources to leave?
CC03.evidence_summary: Childcare access enables economic independence and workforce participation for survivors.
risk_factors: Barriers to workforce participation - childcare (Faller, 2021)
CC03.data_quality_notes: HIGH reliability - Yukon childcare registry data available.

CC04.name: Geographic/social isolation index
CC04.definition_plain: How geographically and socially isolated is this community (considering distance to services, transport options, internet, and cell coverage)?
CC04.domain_question: How does the broader context affect survivor safety?
CC04.evidence_summary: Isolation is a fundamental risk multiplier documented across the literature.
risk_factors: Geographical isolation (Burczycka, 2022; Faller, 2021; Farhall, 2020; Jeffrey, 2019; Kurbatfinski, 2024; Kardashevskaya, 2022; Maxwell, 2024; Hope et al., 2023; CREVAWC, 2021; Youngson, 2021)
Rurality (Farhall, 2020; Kurbatfinski, 2020; Youngson et al., 2021; Heggie et al., 2022)
Long emergency response times (CREVAWC, 2021)
CC04.data_quality_notes: HIGH reliability - composite from infrastructure data.

CC05.name: Community road access type
CC05.definition: Whether community has year-round road access or is fly-in/seasonal access only
CC05.definition_plain: Can you drive to this community year-round, or is it fly-in or seasonal access only?
CC05.tier_rationale: Pathway-critical modifier for all transport/distance indicators
CC05.domain_question: How does the broader context affect survivor safety?
CC05.evidence_summary: Road access fundamentally shapes all service accessibility. Fly-in communities face categorical barriers to emergency response, evacuation, and service access that year-round road communities do not.
risk_factors: Geographical isolation (Burczycka, 2022; Faller, 2021; Farhall, 2020; Jeffrey, 2019)
Lack of year-round roads, inconsistent road conditions (Jeffrey, 2019; Zorn, 2017)
Long emergency response times (CREVAWC, 2021)
protective_factors: Year-round road access enabling emergency evacuation
CC05.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
CC05.rrn_relevance: CRITICAL - Old Crow is only fly-in community; defines baseline access

CC06.name: Extractive industry operations near community
CC06.definition: Count and proximity of active extractive industry operations (mines, quarries, oil/gas) within 100km of community
CC06.definition_plain: How many active mining or oil/gas operations are near this community?
CC06.tier_rationale: RISK DRIVER: Extractive operations are documented risk amplifiers in RRN contexts
CC06.domain_question: How does the broader context affect survivor safety?
CC06.evidence_summary: Extractive industry presence is documented to amplify GBV risk through workforce gender imbalance, transience, and economic disruption.
risk_factors: Living/working in resource extraction industry (Vector Research et al., 2022; Pauktutiit, 2021; CCSG Associates et al., 2021; Hoogeveen, 2020)
Inflated housing costs due to resource development (Flynn, 2023)
Transient workforce reducing community accountability
protective_factors: Strong workplace policies where operations exist (PL07)
CC06.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
CC06.rrn_relevance: CRITICAL - Direct Yukon relevance with active mining operations

EC01.name: Availability of emergency financial aid for GBV survivors
EC01.definition: Whether emergency funds specifically for GBV situations exist
EC01.definition_plain: Is there emergency money available specifically for GBV survivors?
EC01.domain_question: Can survivors access money and resources to leave?
EC01.evidence_summary: Financial dependence is a major barrier to leaving. Emergency funds enable immediate safety actions.
risk_factors: Poverty (Faller, 2021), economic dependence (Kardashevskaya, 2022; CREVAWC, 2021; Youngson et al., 2021)
Financial dependence, including farming as livelihood (Farhall, 2020)
protective_factors: Availability of financial independence programs tailored to victims/survivors in RRN communities
EC01.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - varies by source (shelters, Victim Services, First Nations).
EC01.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Higher costs in RRN contexts increase need

EC02.name: Availability of relocation funds
EC02.definition: Whether financial support for relocation away from abuser exists
EC02.definition_plain: Is there money to help survivors move away from their abuser?
EC02.domain_question: Can survivors access money and resources to leave?
EC02.evidence_summary: Relocation support is essential for survivors leaving abusive situations, particularly when moving away from shared community.
risk_factors: Financial barriers to relocation
Social assistance not reflective of IPV realities (Weeks, 2016; Mantler, 2024)
protective_factors: Income-support reform to reflect needs/barriers unique to IPV (Kardashevskaya, 2022)
Financial support for moving, damage deposits, rent assistance
EC02.data_quality_notes: HIGH reliability - program availability from Housing Corporation is public.
EC02.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Relocation often necessary in small communities

HC01.name: Access to Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner program
HC01.definition: Type of Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner access available
HC01.definition_plain: What kind of access do survivors have to Sexual Assault Nurse Examiners - nurses specially trained to do medical exams and collect evidence after sexual assault?
HC01.domain_question: Do healthcare providers recognize and respond to GBV?
HC01.evidence_summary: SANE access is critical for both immediate healthcare and justice outcomes following sexual violence.
risk_factors: Lack of specialized sexual violence services (Heggie et al., 2022)
protective_factors: Access to specialized SV services (Heggie et al., 2022)
HC01.data_quality_notes: HIGH reliability - program details are public.
HC01.rrn_relevance: CRITICAL - Currently only available in Whitehorse

HC02.name: Number of healthcare workers with IPV training
HC02.definition: Count of healthcare providers with documented IPV/DV training
HC02.definition_plain: How many healthcare workers have training on intimate partner violence?
HC02.domain_question: Do healthcare providers recognize and respond to GBV?
HC02.evidence_summary: Healthcare workers are often first point of contact for survivors. Training improves recognition and appropriate response.
risk_factors: Lack of specialized IPV training for healthcare workers (Rizkalla, 2020; Zorn, 2017; Montesanti, 2024; Mantler, 2022)
Use of biomedical rather than trauma and violence informed approaches (Montesanti, 2024)
protective_factors: Developing specialized IPV training for healthcare workers (Rizkalla, 2020; 2021)
Use of trauma and violence-informed care in health care settings (Mantler, 2022)
HC02.data_quality_notes: LOW reliability - training records are confidential. Would require proxy from training program data.
HC02.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Healthcare often only service available in remote areas

HC03.name: Access to primary healthcare provider
HC03.definition: Whether community has resident or regular visiting primary care
HC03.definition_plain: Does the community have regular access to a doctor or nurse practitioner?
HC03.domain_question: Do healthcare providers recognize and respond to GBV?
HC03.evidence_summary: Primary care access is fundamental to ongoing health support for survivors and may be the only local service available.
risk_factors: Lack of primary health care provider (Mantler, 2022)
Lack of access to health care services, general (Mantler, 2022; Heggie et al., 2022)
Reliance on walk-in clinics (Mantler, 2022)
protective_factors: Access to primary health care provider
Visiting healthcare services in remote communities
key_citations: National Ambulatory Care Reporting System (NACRS) - CIHI
HC03.data_quality_notes: HIGH reliability - CIHI data well documented, updated quarterly. NACRS submission mandated in Yukon.
HC03.rrn_relevance: CRITICAL - Many remote communities rely on visiting providers only

HC04.name: Availability of trauma-informed mental health services
HC04.definition: Whether mental health services with trauma specialization exist
HC04.definition_plain: Are there mental health services available that specialize in trauma?
HC04.domain_question: Do healthcare providers recognize and respond to GBV?
HC04.evidence_summary: Trauma-specialized mental health services are essential for recovery but often unavailable in RRN contexts.
risk_factors: Lack of access to mental health supports (Zorn, 2017; Mantler, 2024)
Lack of options for formal support (Wuerch, 2020; Farhall, 2020; Kurbatfinski, 2024; Youngson et al., 2021; Heggie et al., 2022)
protective_factors: Availability of formal supports for victim/survivors of violence (Weeks, 2016; Saskatchewan, 2025)
Specialized training on violence and trauma-informed approaches (Kardashevskaya, 2022; CREVAWC, 2021)
key_citations: Mental Wellness and Substance Use Services (Yukon)
HC04.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - service inventory from government is public, private practitioners require research compilation.

INT01.name: 2SLGBTQ+ inclusive GBV services
INT01.definition: Whether GBV services have explicit 2SLGBTQ+ inclusive policies and trained staff
INT01.definition_plain: Are GBV services safe and welcoming for 2SLGBTQ+ survivors?
INT01.tier_rationale: PATHWAY-CRITICAL for 2SLGBTQ+ survivors; non-inclusive services may be inaccessible or harmful
INT01.domain_question: Are crisis and counselling services available?
INT01.evidence_summary: 2SLGBTQ+ survivors face unique barriers including fear of outing, heteronormative service assumptions, and lack of appropriate housing options.
risk_factors: Heteronormative service assumptions excluding 2SLGBTQ+ survivors
Fear of outing preventing disclosure (Baker et al., 2021)
Lack of same-gender shelter options
INT01.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
INT01.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Small communities may lack any 2SLGBTQ+ affirming services

INT02.name: Indigenous-led GBV healing options
INT02.definition: Availability of Indigenous-designed and -delivered healing supports for GBV survivors
INT02.definition_plain: Can Indigenous survivors access healing support designed and led by Indigenous people?
INT02.tier_rationale: PATHWAY-CRITICAL for Indigenous survivors; mainstream services may not be culturally safe
INT02.domain_question: Are crisis and counselling services available?
INT02.evidence_summary: Indigenous survivors often prefer culturally-grounded healing approaches over Western clinical models. Indigenous-led services address cultural safety concerns with mainstream systems.
risk_factors: Distrust in mainstream services due to colonial history (DuMont, 2022; Giesbrecht, 2022)
Lack of specialized training in culturally-relevant responses (Rizkalla, 2020; Faller, 2021)
Mainstream services not reflecting Indigenous worldviews
protective_factors: Healthcare providers understanding unique needs of Indigenous survivors (DuMont, 2017)
INT02.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
INT02.rrn_relevance: CRITICAL - Majority Indigenous population in many Yukon communities

INT03.name: Disability accessibility of GBV services
INT03.definition: Physical, sensory, and cognitive accessibility of GBV services
INT03.definition_plain: Can survivors with disabilities access GBV services?
INT03.tier_rationale: PATHWAY-CRITICAL for survivors with disabilities; inaccessible services = no pathway
INT03.domain_question: Are crisis and counselling services available?
INT03.evidence_summary: Survivors with disabilities face compounded barriers including physical inaccessibility, communication barriers, and dependency on abusers for care.
risk_factors: Physical barriers to accessing services
Dependency on abuser for personal care
Communication barriers in disclosure
Disability used as tool of coercive control
INT03.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
INT03.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Accessibility particularly limited in remote locations

INT04.name: Language access for temporary foreign workers
INT04.definition: Whether GBV services are accessible to speakers of languages common among temporary foreign workers
INT04.definition_plain: Can workers who don't speak English or French well access GBV services?
INT04.tier_rationale: PATHWAY-CRITICAL for TFW populations; language barrier = no effective pathway
INT04.domain_question: Are crisis and counselling services available?
INT04.evidence_summary: Temporary foreign workers in extractive industries face language barriers, immigration-linked dependency, and isolation from support systems.
risk_factors: Language barriers when accessing services (Wrathall & Herron, 2021)
Immigration status tied to employer creating power imbalance
Isolation from family and cultural community
Fear of deportation preventing disclosure
protective_factors: Services available in languages common among TFWs (Filipino, Spanish, etc.)
INT04.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
INT04.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Relevant for YESAB assessments of projects using TFW labor

LJ01.name: Access to Victim Services
LJ01.definition: Whether Yukon Victim Services has presence/outreach in community
LJ01.definition_plain: How can survivors access Victim Services in this community?
LJ01.domain_question: Can survivors access legal protection and support?
LJ01.evidence_summary: Victim Services provides critical support including accompaniment, information, and referrals. Access mode (in-person vs. virtual) affects service quality.
risk_factors: Lack of access to legal support (CREVAWC, 2021)
protective_factors: Availability and access to Victim Services (Faller, 2021)
Expansion of DV courts and DV options in existing courts in rural/remote areas (Saskatchewan, 2025)
LJ01.data_quality_notes: HIGH reliability - office locations and outreach schedules are public.
LJ01.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Service presence varies significantly by community

LJ02.name: Legal aid accessibility
LJ02.definition: Legal aid accessibility for family and protection matters accounting for waitlist
LJ02.definition_plain: Can survivors access legal aid for family and protection matters within a reasonable timeframe?
LJ02.domain_question: Can survivors access legal protection and support?
LJ02.evidence_summary: Legal aid is essential for survivors navigating family court, protection orders, and custody matters.
risk_factors: Lack of access to legal support (CREVAWC, 2021)
protective_factors: Availability of legal aid / legal aid reform (Kardashevskaya, 2022; CREVAWC, 2021)
LJ02.data_quality_notes: HIGH reliability - allocations available from Yukon Legal Services Society (semi-public).
LJ02.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Essential for protection orders and custody matters

LJ03.name: Presence of DV-specialized court
LJ03.definition: Whether Domestic Violence Treatment Option Court serves community
LJ03.definition_plain: Is there a specialized domestic violence court (like the Domestic Violence Treatment Option Court, or Domestic Violence Treatment Option Court (DVTO)) that serves this community?
LJ03.domain_question: Can survivors access legal protection and support?
LJ03.evidence_summary: Specialized DV courts improve outcomes by providing appropriate expertise and treatment options.
risk_factors: Standard court processes may not address DV dynamics
protective_factors: Expansion of DV courts and DV options in existing courts in rural/remote areas (Saskatchewan, 2025)
LJ03.data_quality_notes: HIGH reliability - DVTO court schedule and circuit court coverage are public.
LJ03.rrn_relevance: MEDIUM - Whitehorse has DVTO; check circuit coverage for other communities

LJ04.name: Access to alternative justice measures
LJ04.definition: Availability of restorative/Indigenous justice options for GBV
LJ04.definition_plain: Are there restorative or Indigenous justice options available for GBV cases?
LJ04.tier_rationale: MEDIUM priority + critical for Indigenous communities
LJ04.domain_question: Can survivors access legal protection and support?
LJ04.evidence_summary: Restorative and Indigenous justice options are critical for culturally appropriate responses, particularly in Indigenous communities.
risk_factors: Distrust in RCMP, police (Faller, 2021; DuMont, 2022; Giesbrecht, 2022; Mantler, 2024; Rizkalla, 2021; Kardashevskaya, 2022)
LJ04.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - varies by First Nation. Territorial program data is public.

PA01.name: Batterer intervention program availability
PA01.definition: Whether evidence-based batterer intervention programs are accessible
PA01.definition_plain: Are there programs to address the behavior of people who commit violence?
PA01.tier_rationale: PATHWAY-CRITICAL for community safety; absence means no perpetrator intervention
PA01.domain_question: How does the broader context affect survivor safety?
PA01.evidence_summary: Batterer intervention programs are essential for accountability and recurrence prevention. Without them, perpetrators cycle through the system without behavior change.
risk_factors: No accountability mechanisms for perpetrators
Perpetrators returning to community without intervention
Lack of evidence-based programming
protective_factors: Evidence-based batterer intervention programming (Caring Dads, etc.)
Local access reducing barriers to completion
PA01.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
PA01.rrn_relevance: CRITICAL - Currently only available in Whitehorse

PA02.name: Perpetrator housing alternatives
PA02.definition: Whether housing options exist for perpetrators removed from shared residence
PA02.definition_plain: If the person causing harm has to leave the home, is there somewhere for them to go?
PA02.tier_rationale: Affects pathway quality; creates pressure on survivor
PA02.domain_question: Can survivors access emergency and transitional housing?
PA02.evidence_summary: When perpetrators lack housing alternatives, pressure falls on survivors to leave or reconcile. Perpetrator housing options enable survivors to safely remain in their homes.
risk_factors: Perpetrator homelessness increasing contact risk
Pressure on survivor to leave shared residence
Reconciliation driven by housing scarcity not choice
PA02.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
PA02.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Housing scarcity in RRN compounds this gap

PA03.name: Lethality assessment protocol implementation
PA03.definition: Whether Danger Assessment or similar lethality screening is implemented in GBV response
PA03.definition_plain: Do service providers use formal tools to assess whether someone is at risk of being killed?
PA03.tier_rationale: PATHWAY-CRITICAL: Highest-risk survivors may not receive appropriate response without assessment
PA03.domain_question: Do organizations have policies that protect survivors?
PA03.evidence_summary: Lethality assessment tools (e.g., Danger Assessment) identify highest-risk situations enabling prioritized response. Without them, lethal risk cases may not receive appropriate urgency.
risk_factors: Failure to identify high-lethality situations
Under-response to escalating danger
Prior threats to kill victim not flagged (Saskatchewan DVDR, 2025)
PA03.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
PA03.rrn_relevance: CRITICAL - Rural isolation amplifies lethality risk

PA04.name: Firearms removal during protection orders
PA04.definition: Whether protocols exist and are implemented to remove firearms when protection orders are issued
PA04.definition_plain: When a protection order is issued, are firearms actually removed from the person causing harm?
PA04.tier_rationale: PATHWAY-CRITICAL for survival; firearms presence is primary lethality factor
PA04.domain_question: Can survivors access legal protection and support?
PA04.evidence_summary: Firearm presence is the primary lethality risk factor. Protocols to remove firearms during protection orders are essential but often not implemented.
risk_factors: Access to / possession of firearms (Saskatchewan DVDR, 2025)
Prior threats with weapon
Rural gun ownership normalizing access
PA04.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
PA04.rrn_relevance: CRITICAL - High firearm ownership in rural Yukon

PE01.name: Community education campaign presence
PE01.definition: Whether active GBV prevention/education programs operate in community
PE01.definition_plain: Are there programs in the community to educate people about GBV prevention?
PE01.tier_rationale: MEDIUM priority - primary prevention per proposal
PE01.domain_question: How does the broader context affect survivor safety?
PE01.evidence_summary: Primary prevention through education addresses root causes and community attitudes.
risk_factors: Lack of awareness about available resources (Wuerch, 2020; Farhall, 2020; Heggie et al., 2022)
Attitudes and beliefs that condone and/or minimize IPV (Kardashevskaya, 2022; Rizkalla, 2021; Letourneau, 2023; Ross, 2019; Mantler, 2018)
protective_factors: Community education campaigns about GBV (CREVAWC, 2023; Mantler, 2018; Weeks, 2016; Mantler, 2017; Saskatchewan, 2025; Kardashevskaya, 2022; Youngson et al., 2021; Wrathall & Herron, 2021)
key_citations: Federal Gender-based Violence Strategy Annual Reports
PE01.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - requires inventory of initiatives.

PE02.name: Men and boys engagement programs
PE02.definition: Availability of programs engaging men/boys in GBV prevention
PE02.definition_plain: Are there programs that engage men and boys in preventing GBV?
PE02.tier_rationale: MEDIUM priority - primary prevention per proposal
PE02.domain_question: How does the broader context affect survivor safety?
PE02.evidence_summary: Engaging men and boys in prevention addresses perpetration and bystander intervention.
risk_factors: Traditional views about gender roles (Flynn, 2023; Faller, 2021; Farhall, 2020; Jeffrey, 2019)
Misogynistic attitudes (perpetrator factor)
protective_factors: Programming that engages men and boys (Ross, 2019; Wrathall & Herron, 2021)
key_citations: PMC study on engaging men in gender equality (2023)
PE02.data_quality_notes: LOW reliability - relatively rare programs; small sample in existing research.

PL01.name: Policies addressing confidentiality in RRN context
PL01.definition: Whether GBV service providers have explicit policies for small-community confidentiality challenges
PL01.definition_plain: Do service providers have policies for keeping things confidential in rural, remote and northern (RRN) communities where everyone knows each other?
PL01.tier_rationale: MEDIUM priority but core to RRN measurement justice
PL01.domain_question: Do organizations have policies that protect survivors?
PL01.evidence_summary: Small community dynamics create unique confidentiality challenges - 'everyone knows everyone' affects disclosure and service access.
risk_factors: Sense of community surveillance and judgement (Flynn, 2023; Farhall, 2020; CREVAWC, 2021)
Difficulty in keeping shelters private (Zorn, 2017)
Compromised anonymity when disclosing or accessing support (Farhall, 2020; Youngson et al., 2021; Heggie et al., 2022)
protective_factors: Conflict of interest policies unique to IPV / RRN (CREVAWC, 2021)
key_citations: Space for Action Scale (Farhall, Harris, & Woodlock, 2020)
PL01.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - requires policy audit. Framework is qualitative.
PL01.rrn_relevance: CRITICAL - Core measurement justice concern for RRN

PL02.name: Policies addressing multiple-role relationships
PL02.definition: Protocols for when service provider has pre-existing relationship with victim or perpetrator
PL02.definition_plain: Do service providers have policies for when they already know the survivor or abuser personally?
PL02.domain_question: Do organizations have policies that protect survivors?
PL02.evidence_summary: Dual relationships are inevitable in small communities where providers may know both victim and perpetrator personally.
risk_factors: Multiple-role / confidentiality dilemmas due to small community (Rizkalla, 2020; Zorn, 2017; Montesanti, 2024)
Dual relationships (Kardashevskaya, 2022)
PL02.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - requires organizational policy audit.

PL03.name: GBV-specific policies in non-GBV settings
PL03.definition: Whether major employers, schools, health facilities have GBV workplace policies
PL03.definition_plain: Do major employers and schools have policies about GBV?
PL03.tier_rationale: MEDIUM priority + LOW reliability (requires employer survey)
PL03.domain_question: Do organizations have policies that protect survivors?
PL03.evidence_summary: Workplace and institutional policies extend protection beyond specialized services.
risk_factors: Lack of formal policies outlining specialized care for IPV victims (Mantler, 2020; Rizkalla, 2020)
protective_factors: Formalized policies to guide intersectoral collaboration (Mantler, 2022; Carter-Snell et al., 2020)

PL04.name: Level of interagency collaboration
PL04.definition: Existence and activity level of formal coordination mechanisms
PL04.definition_plain: How well do different agencies work together on GBV?
PL04.domain_question: Do organizations have policies that protect survivors?
PL04.evidence_summary: Strong collaboration improves survivor outcomes and prevents gaps in service.
risk_factors: Lack of interagency collaboration (Mantler, 2020; Rizkalla, 2020)
protective_factors: Strong interagency collaboration (Faller, 2021; Jeffrey, 2019; Mantler, 2018; Mantler, 2022; Wuerch, 2021; Wuerch, 2020; Mantler, 2017; Kardashevskaya, 2022; CREVAWC, 2021; Youngson et al., 2021; Carter-Snell et al., 2020)
key_citations: Multiple sources - most comprehensive evidence base
PL04.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - requires assessment of MOUs and committee participation.
PL04.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Essential where services are limited

PL05.name: Evidence of formal referral pathways
PL05.definition: Whether documented referral protocols exist between key services
PL05.definition_plain: Are there clear documented pathways for referring survivors between services?
PL05.domain_question: Do organizations have policies that protect survivors?
PL05.evidence_summary: Clear referral protocols reduce navigation burden on survivors and improve service coordination.
risk_factors: Poor or non-existent referral network (Rizkalla, 2020)
protective_factors: Creating effective referral pathways (Rizkalla, 2020; Mantler, 2018; Mantler, 2017; Heggie et al., 2022)
PL05.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - requires protocol document audit.

PL06.name: Disaster/emergency preparedness in GBV organizations
PL06.definition: Whether GBV service providers have business continuity plans
PL06.definition_plain: Do GBV organizations have plans to keep operating during emergencies?
PL06.domain_question: Do organizations have policies that protect survivors?
PL06.evidence_summary: COVID-19 highlighted vulnerability of GBV services to disruption. Climate emergencies increasingly relevant in north.
risk_factors: Pandemic (Moffitt, 2022; Hope et al., 2021; CREVAWC, 2021)
Natural disasters (CREVAWC, 2021)
Emergency guidelines not translated into local language (Moffitt, 2022)
protective_factors: Business continuity planning for GBV services
PL06.rrn_relevance: MEDIUM - Relevant post-COVID and with increasing wildfires

PL07.name: Workplace GBV policies in extractive industry
PL07.definition: Whether active mine sites have documented GBV/harassment policies
PL07.definition_plain: Do mining companies have policies about GBV and harassment?
PL07.domain_question: Do organizations have policies that protect survivors?
PL07.evidence_summary: Strong evidence links resource extraction to increased GBV risk. Workplace policies are essential preventive measure.
risk_factors: Living / working in resource extraction industry (Vector Research et al., 2022; Paukuutit, 2021; CCSG Associates et al, 2021; Hoogeveen, 2020)
Prevalence/normalization of workplace sexual violence, harassment (Vector Research et al., 2022; Paukuutit, 2021)
Lack of clear policies and reporting mechanisms (Vector Research et al., 2022; Paukuutit, 2021; CCSG Associates et al, 2021)
protective_factors: Clear policies and guidelines on reporting sexual violence/harassment in workplace (Vector Research et al., 2022; Paukuutit, CCSG Associates et al, 2021)
Public education about workplace sexual harassment (Pauktutiit, 2021; Vector et al., 2022)
PL07.data_quality_notes: HIGH reliability - YESAB registry provides access to policy assessments.
PL07.rrn_relevance: CRITICAL - Direct Yukon relevance with active mining operations

PL08.name: Data-sharing agreements between agencies
PL08.definition: Existence of formal agreements enabling coordinated data collection
PL08.definition_plain: Do agencies have agreements to share data with each other?
PL08.domain_question: Do organizations have policies that protect survivors?
PL08.evidence_summary: Data sharing enables coordinated response and system-level analysis while respecting privacy.
risk_factors: Data gaps and/or failure to collect key information (Giesbrecht, 2023)
Poor or limited data collection methods (Giesbrecht, 2023)
protective_factors: Standardized methods of front-line agency data collection (Giesbrecht, 2023)
Legislation that allows collection of relevant risk assessment data (Saskatchewan, 2025)
PL08.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - foundational for future measurement.

PRV01.name: Healthy relationships education in schools
PRV01.definition: Whether K-12 schools implement evidence-based healthy relationships curriculum
PRV01.definition_plain: Do schools teach students about healthy relationships and consent?
PRV01.domain_question: How does the broader context affect survivor safety?
PRV01.evidence_summary: School-based healthy relationships education is evidence-based primary prevention addressing attitudes and norms before violence occurs.
risk_factors: Attitudes and beliefs that condone and/or minimize IPV (Kardashevskaya, 2022; Rizkalla, 2021; Letourneau, 2023)
Traditional views about gender roles (Flynn, 2023; Faller, 2021)
PRV01.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
PRV01.rrn_relevance: MEDIUM - Prevention infrastructure for long-term change

PRV02.name: Bystander intervention training availability
PRV02.definition: Whether bystander intervention training programs are accessible in community
PRV02.definition_plain: Can community members learn how to safely intervene when they see warning signs of GBV?
PRV02.domain_question: How does the broader context affect survivor safety?
PRV02.evidence_summary: Bystander intervention training enables community members to recognize warning signs and safely intervene before violence escalates.
risk_factors: Lack of awareness about warning signs
Community members uncertain how to intervene
Sense that violence is private matter
PRV02.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
PRV02.rrn_relevance: MEDIUM - Particularly relevant for workplace settings (mining)

PRV03.name: Alcohol policy environment
PRV03.definition: Regulatory environment for alcohol access in community
PRV03.definition_plain: How is alcohol access regulated in this community?
PRV03.domain_question: How does the broader context affect survivor safety?
PRV03.evidence_summary: Alcohol is a documented risk driver for IPV severity and lethality. Community-level alcohol policy environment shapes population-level risk.
risk_factors: Excessive alcohol and/or drug use (Saskatchewan DVDR, 2025)
High alcohol outlet density
No restrictions on alcohol access
PRV03.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
PRV03.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Several Yukon communities have alcohol restrictions

PRV04.name: Substance use treatment access
PRV04.definition_plain: Can people access treatment for alcohol or drug problems in or near this community?
PRV04.domain_question: Do healthcare providers recognize and respond to GBV?
PRV04.evidence_summary: Substance use treatment access addresses a major co-occurring factor. Lack of treatment options perpetuates cycles of violence.
risk_factors: Excessive alcohol and/or drug use (Saskatchewan DVDR, 2025)
No local treatment options
Long waitlists for residential treatment
key_citations: Mental Wellness and Substance Use Services (Yukon)
PRV04.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
PRV04.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Treatment access limited outside Whitehorse

PRV05.name: RCMP detachment turnover rate
PRV05.definition: Annual turnover rate of RCMP officers at community detachment
PRV05.definition_plain: How often do RCMP officers in this community get replaced?
PRV05.domain_question: Can survivors access legal protection and support?
PRV05.evidence_summary: RCMP turnover affects community trust and investigative continuity. High turnover means officers leave before building relationships or seeing cases through.
risk_factors: Distrust in RCMP, police (Faller, 2021; DuMont, 2022; Giesbrecht, 2022; Mantler, 2024)
Officers unfamiliar with community context
Case file discontinuity
PRV05.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
PRV05.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Named in original proposal as priority

PX01.name: Gas prices relative to territorial average
PX01.definition: Ratio of local fuel prices to Whitehorse baseline
PX01.definition_plain: How much more expensive is gas in this community compared to Whitehorse?
PX01.domain: Getting Where You Need to Go
PX01.domain_question: Can survivors travel to services safely?
PX01.evidence_summary: Fuel prices directly impact travel costs, which compound barriers to service access in RRN contexts.
risk_factors: Financial barriers to accessing distant services
Requirement to travel long distance (Flynn, 2023; Farhall, 2020)
High transportation costs
PX01.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
PX01.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Proxy for travel cost barriers

PX02.name: Median household income by community
PX02.definition: Community-level median income relative to territorial median
PX02.definition_plain: What is the median household income in this community?
PX02.domain_question: Can survivors access money and resources to leave?
PX02.evidence_summary: Community income levels contextualize economic capacity for survivors to access services, secure housing, and achieve independence.
risk_factors: Poverty (Faller, 2021)
Economic dependence (Kardashevskaya, 2022; CREVAWC, 2021)
Limited employment options in community
PX02.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.

PX03.name: Financial services presence
PX03.definition: Whether community has bank or credit union physical presence
PX03.definition_plain: Is there a bank or credit union in this community?
PX03.domain_question: Can survivors access money and resources to leave?
PX03.evidence_summary: Banking access is essential for financial safety planning—opening accounts without abuser knowledge, accessing funds, building independence.
risk_factors: No local banking access
Financial control by abuser enabled by limited options
Cannot access funds without traveling
PX03.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
PX03.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Many communities lack any banking presence

PX04.name: Health centre operational status
PX04.definition: Whether community health centre is currently operational or has recent closures
PX04.definition_plain: Is the health centre in this community currently open and staffed?
PX04.domain_question: Do healthcare providers recognize and respond to GBV?
PX04.evidence_summary: Health centre closures or reduced hours directly impact emergency response and ongoing healthcare access.
risk_factors: Intermittent / inconsistent services due to partial staffing (Zorn, 2017)
Health centre closures
Reduced operating hours
PX04.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.

PX05.name: Emergency department wait times (WGH)
PX05.definition: Average wait time at Whitehorse General Hospital emergency department
PX05.definition_plain: How long are emergency wait times at WGH?
PX05.domain_question: Do healthcare providers recognize and respond to GBV?
PX05.evidence_summary: Whitehorse General Hospital wait times contextualize emergency healthcare access for communities that must travel there.
risk_factors: Long emergency wait times
Evidence collection window passing (SANE)
Delayed treatment of injuries
PX05.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.

SH01.name: Number of emergency shelters in community
SH01.definition: Count of facilities providing emergency overnight accommodation for GBV survivors
SH01.definition_plain: How many emergency shelters can survivors go to in this community?
SH01.domain_question: Can survivors access emergency and transitional housing?
SH01.evidence_summary: Access to emergency shelter is consistently identified as a critical protective factor across the literature. Lack of shelter access is associated with women remaining in or returning to violent situations.
risk_factors: Long waitlists to access services (Mantler, 2024; Heggie et al., 2022)
Shelters do not reflect unique needs of rural women (Weeks, 2016)
Difficulty in keeping shelters private, hidden in RRN contexts (Zorn, 2017)
Lack of emergency housing (Moffitt, 2022; Zorn, 2017; Farhall, 2020)
protective_factors: Access to shelters / safe houses (CREVAWC, 2021; Faller, 2021; Hope et al., 2023; Jeffrey, 2019; Kardashevskaya, 2022)
Access to specialized GBV-specific services (Carter-Snell et al., 2020)
SH01.data_quality_notes: Previous surveys by Women's Shelters Canada and ESVA are well documented but primarily in PDF format. Timeliness is challenging as survey data can be one-off or funding-dependent.
SH01.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Critical infrastructure gap in northern/remote communities

SH02.name: Number of GBV-designated second-stage housing units
SH02.definition: Count of transitional housing units with GBV-specific mandates or formal survivor allocation agreements
SH02.definition_plain: How many transitional housing units are specifically designated for GBV survivors in this community?
SH02.domain_question: Can survivors access emergency and transitional housing?
SH02.evidence_summary: Transitional housing is essential for survivors moving from emergency shelter to independent living. Literature identifies housing stability as a key factor in preventing returns to abusive situations.
risk_factors: Lack of affordable housing (CCSG Associates et al., 2021; Flynn, 2023; Hope et al., 2023; Maxwell, 2024; Moffitt, 2022)
Inflated housing costs due to resource development (Flynn, 2023)
Housing market pressure from short-term rentals and gentrification (Mantler, 2024)
protective_factors: Availability of safe, affordable housing options
SH02.data_quality_notes: HART dataset from UBC is well-maintained with good methodology. Last update 2021; next release expected 2026. Pre-pandemic data raises some reliability concerns.
SH02.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Limited housing stock in northern communities

SH03.name: Shelter access barriers
SH03.definition: Shelter access barriers measured via capacity utilization and wait time data
SH03.definition_plain: How often are survivors unable to access shelter when they need it, and how long do they wait?
SH03.domain_question: Can survivors access emergency and transitional housing?
SH03.evidence_summary: Service accessibility timing is critical during crisis. Long waitlists are documented as a barrier to safety.
risk_factors: Long waitlists to access services (Mantler, 2024; Heggie et al., 2022)
Intermittent / inconsistent services due to partial staffing (Zorn, 2017)
SH03.data_quality_notes: Requires shelter intake data. Aggregate-only access due to confidentiality. ESVA Waitlist Survey may serve as proxy.
SH03.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Extended wait times exacerbated by limited options

SH04.name: Pet care options for survivors
SH04.definition: Whether survivors can avoid abandoning companion animals when leaving, including shelter pet accommodation, foster networks, and temporary care arrangements
SH04.definition_plain: Can survivors keep their pets safe when they leave? This includes shelters that accept pets, foster programs for pets, or other arrangements so survivors do not have to abandon their animals.
SH04.tier_rationale: MEDIUM priority but critical northern context
SH04.domain_question: Can survivors access emergency and transitional housing?
SH04.evidence_summary: Strong evidence that concern for animal welfare prevents women from leaving abusive situations. Pet ownership is particularly common in rural/northern contexts.
risk_factors: Dealing with or needing to house larger animals/livestock (Wuerch 2020; 2021)
Financial barriers related to caring for livestock (Giesbrecht, 2022; Wuerch, 2021)
Challenges in animal safekeeping with confidentiality concerns (Wuerch, 2021)
protective_factors: Access to pet-friendly DV shelters (Giesbrecht, 2022; Wuerch, 2021; Wuerch, 2020)
Safety planning that includes animal care (Giesbrecht, 2022)
Ability of family/friends to board animals (Wuerch, 2021)
SH04.data_quality_notes: Low quality indicator nationally - no current survey collects this specific to Yukon. Academic surveys indicate 10-20% of those experiencing homelessness have pets.
SH04.rrn_relevance: CRITICAL - Animals/livestock common in rural/northern contexts; major barrier to leaving

SH05.name: Distance to nearest shelter from community centre
SH05.definition: Kilometres from community's main intersection/centre to nearest GBV shelter
SH05.definition_plain: How far do survivors have to travel to reach the nearest shelter?
SH05.domain_question: Can survivors access emergency and transitional housing?
SH05.evidence_summary: Geographic isolation is consistently identified as a risk factor. Distance to services compounds barriers for survivors in remote communities.
risk_factors: Geographical isolation (Burczycka, 2022; Faller, 2021; Farhall, 2020; Jeffrey, 2019; Kurbatfinski, 2024)
Requirement to travel long distance to access support (Flynn, 2023; Farhall, 2020)
Long emergency response times (CREVAWC, 2021)
protective_factors: Availability of travel funds to support access to services (Faller, 2021)
key_citations: Jeffrey et al. (2019) - Domestic Violence and Homicide in RRN Communities
SH05.data_quality_notes: HIGH reliability - calculable via GIS/Google Maps. Static indicator updated only when new shelters open.

SH06.name: Availability of pet-friendly rental housing
SH06.definition: Proportion of rental housing stock that permits pets
SH06.definition_plain: What percentage of rental housing allows pets?
SH06.domain_question: Can survivors access emergency and transitional housing?
SH06.evidence_summary: Housing options for survivors with animals are limited, creating barriers to permanent relocation away from abusers.
risk_factors: Lack of pet-friendly rental housing (Giesbrecht, 2022)
SH06.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - estimates available from CMHC and housing authority data.
SH06.rrn_relevance: MEDIUM - Relevant where animal ownership is common

SQ01.name: Trauma-informed mental health services (quality)
SQ01.definition: Degree to which available MH services meet trauma-informed standards
SQ01.definition_plain: How well do mental health services actually meet trauma-informed standards?
SQ01.domain_question: Do healthcare providers recognize and respond to GBV?
SQ01.evidence_summary: Quality assessment goes beyond availability to actual trauma-informed practice.
risk_factors: Use of biomedical rather than trauma and violence informed approaches (Montesanti, 2024)
protective_factors: Use of trauma and violence-informed care (Mantler, 2022)
SQ01.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Quality matters as much as availability

SQ02.name: GBV information in rural-appropriate formats
SQ02.definition: Whether GBV service information distributed via formats accessible without internet
SQ02.definition_plain: In this community, can survivors learn about services without needing internet access (e.g., through print, radio, posters)?
SQ02.tier_rationale: MEDIUM priority but core to RRN accessibility
SQ02.domain_question: Are crisis and counselling services available?
SQ02.evidence_summary: Information accessibility without internet is essential in RRN contexts where connectivity is unreliable.
risk_factors: Lack of awareness about available resources (Wuerch, 2020; Farhall, 2020; Heggie et al., 2022)
Poor quality internet service (Mantler, 2024)
protective_factors: Community education about GBV services (Mantler, 2018; Weeks, 2016)
SQ02.data_quality_notes: HIGH reliability - distribution methods can be audited directly.
SQ02.rrn_relevance: CRITICAL - Internet unreliable in many Yukon communities

SQ03.name: Services available in Indigenous languages
SQ03.definition: Whether GBV services available in local First Nation languages
SQ03.definition_plain: Can survivors access services in their First Nation language?
SQ03.tier_rationale: MEDIUM priority but core to Indigenous access
SQ03.domain_question: Are crisis and counselling services available?
SQ03.evidence_summary: Language access is fundamental to culturally appropriate service delivery.
risk_factors: Language barriers when accessing services (Wrathall & Herron, 2021)
Language/cultural barriers (Victim factors)
protective_factors: Availability of services in language of choice
SQ03.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - requires service provider inquiry.
SQ03.rrn_relevance: HIGH - 8 First Nation language families in Yukon

SQ04.name: Level of service integration
SQ04.definition: Degree to which services are co-located or require multiple separate contacts
SQ04.definition_plain: How many different places do survivors have to go to get help?
SQ04.domain_question: Are crisis and counselling services available?
SQ04.evidence_summary: Integrated services reduce navigation burden on survivors who are already in crisis.
risk_factors: Multiple contacts required to access support
protective_factors: Integration of health/social services within shelter - HUB model (Jeffrey, 2019; Mantler, 2018; Mantler, 2022)
SQ04.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - requires key informant assessment.
SQ04.rrn_relevance: MEDIUM - Whitehorse more integrated than rural

SQ05.name: Effectiveness of Emergency Protection Orders
SQ05.definition: Rate at which EPOs are granted and enforced
SQ05.definition_plain: Do Emergency Protection Orders actually get granted and enforced?
SQ05.tier_rationale: MEDIUM priority + LOW reliability (RCMP data via ATIP)
SQ05.domain_question: Can survivors access legal protection and support?
SQ05.evidence_summary: Legal protection only works if orders are granted and enforced.
risk_factors: Legal protections not enforced
protective_factors: EPOs that reflect understanding of unique needs (Giesbrecht, 2022)
EPOs that contain explicit descriptions of stalking behaviours (Kurbatfinski, 2024)
SQ05.data_quality_notes: LOW reliability - RCMP enforcement data requires ATIP request.
SQ05.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Enforcement challenging in remote communities

SQ06.name: Community readiness for new GBV programs
SQ06.definition: Assessment of implementation feasibility for new interventions
SQ06.definition_plain: Is the community ready to support new GBV programs?
SQ06.domain_question: How does the broader context affect survivor safety?
SQ06.evidence_summary: Implementation success depends on community capacity and readiness.
risk_factors: Program implementation without community readiness assessment
protective_factors: Community readiness assessment before program implementation
SQ06.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - requires primary research (key informant interviews).

SS01.name: Number of GBV-specific services in community
SS01.definition: Count of organizations with explicit GBV service mandate
SS01.definition_plain: How many organizations in this community specifically help GBV survivors?
SS01.domain_question: Are crisis and counselling services available?
SS01.evidence_summary: Service availability is foundational to survivor support. Multiple services provide options and specialized support.
risk_factors: Poor or non-existent referral network due to lack of services (Rizkalla, 2020)
Lack of options for formal support (Wuerch, 2020; Farhall, 2020)
protective_factors: Access to specialized GBV-specific services (Carter-Snell et al., 2020)
key_citations: Yukon Status of Women Council service directory
SS01.data_quality_notes: HIGH reliability - service directories are public and maintained.
SS01.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Most communities have few or no GBV-specific services

SS02.name: Availability of virtual service options
SS02.definition: Whether GBV services can be accessed remotely
SS02.definition_plain: Can survivors access GBV services by phone or video?
SS02.domain_question: Are crisis and counselling services available?
SS02.evidence_summary: Virtual services can bridge geographic gaps but require technology infrastructure.
risk_factors: Poor quality internet service (Mantler, 2024)
Geographic isolation limiting in-person access
protective_factors: Using technology to bridge service gaps created by geography (Mantler, 2018; Mantler, 2024)
SS02.data_quality_notes: HIGH reliability - service modality can be audited directly.

SS03.name: Wait time for counselling services
SS03.definition: Average days from referral to first counselling appointment
SS03.definition_plain: How long do survivors wait to see a counsellor?
SS03.domain_question: Are crisis and counselling services available?
SS03.evidence_summary: Timely access to counselling is critical for recovery. Long wait times can exacerbate trauma.
risk_factors: Long waitlists to access services (Mantler, 2024; Heggie et al., 2022)
protective_factors: Timely access to mental health support
SS03.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - requires provider survey data. Confidential aggregate only.
SS03.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Limited providers means longer waits

SS04.name: 24/7 crisis line access
SS04.definition: Whether 24/7 crisis support is accessible from community
SS04.definition_plain: Can survivors call a crisis line any time day or night?
SS04.domain_question: Are crisis and counselling services available?
SS04.evidence_summary: Round-the-clock crisis support is essential as crises don't follow business hours.
risk_factors: Lack of emergency or crisis supports
SS04.data_quality_notes: HIGH reliability - coverage and hours are public information.
SS04.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Note if long-distance charges apply from remote areas

TR01.name: Level of public transit service
TR01.definition: Level of public transit service availability in community
TR01.definition_plain: How much public transit is available in this community?
TR01.domain: Getting Where You Need to Go
TR01.domain_question: Can survivors travel to services safely?
TR01.evidence_summary: Transportation access is fundamental to service access. Lack of public transit in rural/remote areas severely limits options for survivors.
risk_factors: Lack of affordable and accessible transportation (Moffitt, 2022; Faller, 2021; Zorn, 2017; Farhall, 2020; CREVAWC, 2021; Pauktutiit, 2021; Youngson et al., 2021; Heggie et al., 2022)
Reliance on 'unsafe' alternative transportation methods like hitchhiking (Winnicki, 2024)
Cancellation of public transportation (Winnicki, 2024)
protective_factors: Affordable and accessible public transportation (CCSG Associates et al., 2021; Hanson, 2021; Hope et al., 2023; Jeffrey, 2019; Winnicki, 2024; Kardashevskaya, 2022)
TR01.data_quality_notes: Living wage report published yearly. Hard to apply outside Whitehorse. Community-driven research methodology.
TR01.rrn_relevance: CRITICAL - Most RRN communities lack public transit

TR02.name: Existence of emergency transportation options
TR02.definition: Availability of crisis transportation (not requiring personal vehicle)
TR02.definition_plain: Can survivors get emergency transportation without needing their own car?
TR02.domain: Getting Where You Need to Go
TR02.domain_question: Can survivors travel to services safely?
TR02.evidence_summary: Crisis transportation that doesn't require personal vehicle ownership is essential for survivors in urgent situations.
risk_factors: Lack of year-round roads, inconsistent road conditions (Jeffrey, 2019; Zorn, 2017)
protective_factors: Local, municipal, province-led or grassroots initiatives to provide transportation (Winnicki, 2024; Saskatchewan, 2025)
Transportation policy integrating intersectional, transportation justice framework (Hanson et al., 2021; Winnicki, 2024)
TR02.data_quality_notes: Semi-public data from Victim Services and shelters. Requires direct inquiry.
TR02.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Essential where personal vehicles may not be accessible

TR03.name: Distance to nearest hospital with Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner
TR03.definition: Kilometres to nearest Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner program
TR03.definition_plain: How far is the nearest hospital with a Sexual Assault Nurse Examiner - a nurse specially trained to do medical exams and collect evidence after sexual assault?
TR03.domain: Getting Where You Need to Go
TR03.domain_question: Can survivors travel to services safely?
TR03.evidence_summary: Access to Sexual Assault Nurse Examiners is critical for forensic evidence collection within the 72-120 hour window post-assault.
risk_factors: Lack of specialized sexual violence services (Heggie et al., 2022)
Requirement to travel long distance to access support (Flynn, 2023)
protective_factors: Outreach to Indigenous communities on hospital-based SANE programs (DuMont, 2017)
TR03.data_quality_notes: HIGH reliability - SANE program locations are public knowledge. Currently only Whitehorse General Hospital in Yukon.
TR03.rrn_relevance: CRITICAL - Most Yukon communities require significant travel

TR04.name: Availability of travel funds for GBV services
TR04.definition: Whether dedicated travel subsidy exists for GBV service access
TR04.definition_plain: Is there money available to help survivors pay for travel to get services?
TR04.domain: Getting Where You Need to Go
TR04.domain_question: Can survivors travel to services safely?
TR04.evidence_summary: Financial support for travel is essential in contexts where services are geographically distant.
risk_factors: Financial barriers to accessing distant services
Economic burden of accessing private services (Heggie et al., 2022)
protective_factors: Availability of travel funds to support access to services (Faller, 2021)
TR04.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - varies by Nation for First Nations travel support. Semi-public from Victim Services.
TR04.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Essential for service access from remote communities

TR05.name: Number of transportation options for crisis situations
TR05.definition: Count of distinct crisis transportation mechanisms available
TR05.definition_plain: How many different ways can survivors get emergency transportation?
TR05.domain: Getting Where You Need to Go
TR05.domain_question: Can survivors travel to services safely?
TR05.evidence_summary: Multiple transportation options increase accessibility and provide backup when primary options unavailable.
risk_factors: Limited transportation options compound isolation
TR05.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - requires compilation from multiple sources.
TR05.rrn_relevance: MEDIUM - Redundancy important in RRN contexts

WF01.name: Staff turnover in GBV sector
WF01.definition: Annual turnover rate in frontline GBV positions
WF01.definition_plain: How often do staff leave GBV organizations?
WF01.domain_question: Do organizations have policies that protect survivors?
WF01.evidence_summary: High turnover undermines service quality and survivor trust. Workforce stability is a capacity indicator.
risk_factors: Intermittent / inconsistent services due to partial staffing, seasonal staffing (Zorn, 2017)
Staffing challenges - retention, burnout (Montesanti, 2024)
WF01.data_quality_notes: LOW reliability - requires confidential workforce survey.
WF01.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Turnover particularly problematic in remote postings

WF02.name: Workforce health indicators
WF02.definition: Vacancy rates and burnout indicators in GBV sector
WF02.definition_plain: Are GBV organizations fully staffed and are workers burning out?
WF02.domain_question: Do organizations have policies that protect survivors?
WF02.evidence_summary: Burnout and vacancies predict service availability. Workforce wellbeing affects service quality.
risk_factors: Staffing challenges - retention, burnout (Montesanti, 2024)
WF02.data_quality_notes: LOW reliability - requires anonymous workforce survey.
WF02.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Burnout common in under-resourced northern services

WF03.name: Access to specialized GBV training
WF03.definition: Whether local/accessible GBV training opportunities exist for workforce
WF03.definition_plain: Can workers access specialized GBV training locally?
WF03.domain_question: Do organizations have policies that protect survivors?
WF03.evidence_summary: Ongoing professional development maintains service quality and prevents secondary trauma.
risk_factors: Lack of specialized training (Rizkalla, 2020; Kardashevskaya, 2022)
protective_factors: Training on risk factors for IP/DH (Giesbrecht, 2023; Youngson et. al, 2021)
Other professional development opportunities (Carter-Snell et al., 2020)
WF03.data_quality_notes: MEDIUM reliability - training calendars available from HSS.
WF03.rrn_relevance: MEDIUM - Training access often requires travel

WF04.name: Clinical debriefing opportunities
WF04.definition: Whether structured debriefing/supervision exists for GBV workers
WF04.definition_plain: Do GBV workers have access to professional debriefing and supervision?
WF04.domain_question: Do organizations have policies that protect survivors?
WF04.evidence_summary: Structured supervision mitigates vicarious trauma in GBV workers.
risk_factors: Vicarious trauma without support structures
protective_factors: Opportunities for clinical debriefing related to GBV cases

WF05.name: Indigenous cultural safety training in healthcare
WF05.definition: Whether healthcare workers have completed Indigenous cultural safety training
WF05.definition_plain: Have healthcare workers completed Indigenous cultural safety training?
WF05.domain_question: Do healthcare providers recognize and respond to GBV?
WF05.evidence_summary: Cultural safety training is essential for appropriate service delivery to Indigenous survivors.
risk_factors: Lack of specialized training in cultural safety and culturally-relevant responses to IPV (Rizkalla, 2020; Faller, 2021; Zorn, 2017; Montesanti, 2024)
protective_factors: Healthcare providers understanding unique needs of Indigenous survivors (DuMont, 2017; Rizkalla, 2021)
Specialized training on sexual violence, Indigenous survivors in health care settings (DuMont, 2017)
WF05.data_quality_notes: LOW reliability - training completions are confidential.
WF05.rrn_relevance: CRITICAL - Yukon Indigenous population requires culturally safe services

YRA01.name: Projected workforce gender ratio change
YRA01.definition: Projected change in community/regional gender ratio due to project workforce
YRA01.definition_plain: How much will this project change the ratio of men to women in the area?
YRA01.tier_rationale: RISK DRIVER: Gender ratio imbalance directly associated with GBV prevalence
YRA01.domain_question: How does the broader context affect survivor safety?
YRA01.evidence_summary: Workforce gender imbalance is a documented driver of increased GBV risk. Projects bringing predominantly male workforces into communities shift local gender ratios.
risk_factors: Presence of predominantly male workforce (Pauktutiit, 2021; CCSG Associates, 2021)
Shift in community gender ratio
Resource extraction workforce dynamics
YRA01.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
YRA01.rrn_relevance: CRITICAL - Primary YESAB risk assessment indicator

YRA02.name: Rotational workforce proportion
YRA02.definition: Proportion of project workforce on rotational (FIFO/DIDO) schedules
YRA02.definition_plain: What proportion of workers will be temporary or rotational rather than community residents?
YRA02.tier_rationale: Risk amplifier; transience reduces social accountability
YRA02.domain_question: How does the broader context affect survivor safety?
YRA02.evidence_summary: Rotational workforces (fly-in/fly-out, drive-in/drive-out) create transience that reduces community accountability and integration.
risk_factors: Transient workforce not integrated into community
Reduced accountability for behavior
Economic relationships without social accountability
YRA02.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
YRA02.rrn_relevance: HIGH - Common in Yukon mining operations

YRA03.name: Historical GBV pattern in comparable projects
YRA03.definition: Evidence from comparable extractive projects regarding GBV pattern changes
YRA03.definition_plain: What happened to GBV indicators in other communities when similar projects arrived?
YRA03.tier_rationale: Direct evidence of risk amplification pattern
YRA03.domain_question: How does the broader context affect survivor safety?
YRA03.evidence_summary: Historical evidence from comparable extractive projects provides empirical basis for risk projection.
risk_factors: Documented GBV increases in comparable projects
Pattern of extractive industry impacts
protective_factors: Projects with demonstrated no-harm track record
YRA03.data_quality_notes: NEW - Evidence populated from synthesis and research.
YRA03.rrn_relevance: CRITICAL - Evidence base for YESAB arguments
